newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish muscle vital in for Retevision bid groups.
newsitem.headline: Spanish muscle vital in for Retevision bid groups.

text.p: The fight to become Spain's number two telecoms operator favours the bidder with the most local muscle , analysts said on Monday as final offers for the privatisation of Retevision were submitted.
"The idea is to maintain Retevision's Spanishness and a lot will depend on the weight of the Spanish partners," said Ignacio Cornejo, telecoms specialist at brokers Beta Capital.

Four consortia with a range of foreign and Spanish partners expressed interest in the state's sale of 60 percent of Retevision and its license to provide basic telephone service, but only two handed in completed bids on Monday.
Both the Opera group formed by Spanish bank BCH, France Telecom and U.S. operator Sprint, and the group formed by Endesa and Italy's Stet were seen as strong contenders.
But the presence of 66-percent state-owned electricity utility Endesa, which is one of Spain's biggest companies and has miles of existing networks, was seen as giving extra heft to the latter group.
"Endesa is a natural partner for a second telecoms operator in terms of infrastructure and its strong financial position," Cornejo said.
The government, which is supposed to reach a decision within two weeks, will also be looking for cash, so the size of the financial offer is weighted heavily according to the bid terms.
Retevision's privatisation is one of a series Spain is undertaking to put it in a strong financial position ahead of entrance into Europe's economic and monetary union.

Spain's Contracts Commission will give 40 percent of the weighting to the highest bidder, with 20 percent for infrastructure and networks, 20 percent for finanical backing and strategic plan, 10 percent for experience, and 10 percent for service improvement and benefit to the Spanish economy.
Bidders need to offer at least 45.6 billion pesetas with an additional 10 percent capital increase, but beyond that views are mixed on how much Retevision is worth.

A key factor in the successful transformation of Retevision, a television broadcaster with 1,200 skilled workers and 18,000 km (11,000 miles) of digital networks, into a strong competitor for the former state monopoly Telefonica de Espana will be the unknown cost of hooking up to Telefonica's networks.
The government, Telefonica and Retevision are in the process of negotiating this rate.

The consortium that can most quickly develop its own networks will have a leg up on future competition. Spain is offering a third license next year and liberalising the whole market by the end of 1998.

"It's impossible to guess how well any given group is going to do. We simply don't have enough information about investment plans, the cost of interconnection, the phone rates etc.," another Spanish telecoms analyst said.
"But the group with the most existing network capacity will have a definite advantage."
The second analyst, who did not wish to be named, also said the Endesa/Stet group looked stronger.

The consortium, which has to limit the size of its financial offer because it includes a number of savings banks with restrictive charters, has already said it will stick together to vie for the third license if it loses out on Retevision.
"It (the economic offer) shouldn't be the determining factor," a director with the Endesa/Stet group said. "The most important thing is to ensure the future of the company."
Endesa/Stet plans a heavy investment schedule with other Spanish industrial firms that will add value to Retevision and create jobs.
